source_text: Καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον λέγω, οὐκ ἀπιστῶν ὁ Χριστιανὸς τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ, ἀλλὰ δυσωπῶν ἐκ τῶν κοινῇ ἡμῖν πεπιστευμένων ὅτι πολλῷ οὗτος ἐκείνων ἄξιός ἐστι τοῦ πιστεύεσθαι τοιαῦτα λέγων ἑωρακέναι καὶ ὡς εἰκὸς παραδοὺς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἣν εἶδεν ὄψιν καὶ τὴν φωνὴν ἧς ἤκουσεν. ἄλλος δ᾿ ἄν τις εἴποι ὅτι οὐ πάντες τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἤκουσαν ταῦτα διηγουμένου οἱ ἀναγράψαντες τὰ περὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς καὶ τῆς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ διδάξαν Μωϋσέα πνεῦμα τὴν πρεσβυτέραν αὐτοῦ ἱστορίαν, ἀρξαμένην ἀπὸ τῆς κοσμογενείας μέχρι τῆς κατὰ τὸν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ, τοῦτ᾿ ἐδίδαξε καὶ τοὺς γράψαντας τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τὸ γενόμενον παράδοξον κατὰ τὸν χρόνον τοῦ βαπτίσματος Ἰησοῦ. ὁ δὲ κοσμηθεὶς χαρίσματι καλουμένῳ „λόγῳ σοφίας“ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν διηγήσεται τῆς ἀνοίξεως τῶν οὐρανῶν καὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς, καὶ ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλου τινὸς ζῴου εἴδει ἢ τούτου ἐφάνη τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ. περὶ τούτου δὲ οὐκ ἀπαιτεῖ νῦν ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος διηγήσασθαι· τὸ γὰρ προκείμενόν ἐστιν ἐλέγξαι τὸν Κέλσον οὐχ ὑγιῶς Ἰουδαίῳ περιθέντα μετὰ τοιῶνδε λόγων ἀπιστίαν περὶ πράγματος, κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς γενομένου μᾶλλον παρὰ τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου.
pass_a_gloss: And I say these things to the Jew, not because the Christian disbelieves Ezekiel and Isaiah, but because, being reverent towards what has been commonly entrusted to us, this one is much more worthy of being believed when saying such things as he has seen and, as is likely, handing down to the disciples the vision he saw and the voice he heard. Another might say that not all of Jesus' disciples heard him recounting these things, those who wrote down the things about the appearance of the dove and the voice from heaven; but the Spirit that taught Moses, the older history, which began from the creation of the world until the time of Abraham, his father, also taught those who wrote the gospel, the paradox that occurred at the time of Jesus' baptism. And the one adorned with the charisma called 'word of wisdom' will recount the reason for the opening of the heavens and the appearance of the dove, and why the Holy Spirit appeared to Jesus in the form of this animal and not another. But our discussion does not now require us to recount this; for what is at hand is to refute Celsus, who, like a Jew, has improperly thrown in unbelief about a matter, which has likely occurred more than what was believed by him.

pass_b_english: I address these words to the Jew, not because the Christian disbelieves Ezekiel and Isaiah, but out of reverence for what has been commonly entrusted to us: that this one is far more worthy of belief when he says he has seen such things and, as is likely, handed down to the disciples the vision he saw and the voice he heard (Matthew 3:16-17). Another might object that not all who heard Jesus recount these things were the ones who wrote down the account of the dove's appearance and the voice from heaven. Yet the same Spirit that taught Moses the earlier history — beginning from the creation of the world (Genesis 1:1) down to the time of Abraham his father — also taught the gospel writers the paradox that occurred at the time of Jesus' baptism. And the one adorned with the charism called 'word of wisdom' will recount the reason for the opening of the heavens and the appearance of the dove, and why the Holy Spirit appeared to Jesus in the form of this creature and not another. Our present discussion does not require us to recount that now; for the task at hand is to refute Celsus, who has improperly, like a Jew, thrown in unbelief about a matter that has more likely occurred than what he believed.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex syntax of the first sentence. Pass B's inclusion of scripture citations (Matthew 3:16-17 and Genesis 1:1) for the alluded events is appropriate and matches the Greek content. The translation of 'δυσωπῶν' as 'being reverent' (Pass A) or 'out of reverence' (Pass B) is a valid interpretation of the specific lexical choice in this context.
